IRS Form 990 e-file · Schedule I Part II & 990-PF Part XV

Hawaii Food Flows

Food and cash moving between Hawaii food and agriculture nonprofits, the agencies and farms they support, and the national networks and funders that supply them. Each line is a grant one organization reported giving another, valued as filed. How to read this

This page maps where food and the money behind it move among Hawaii food and agriculture nonprofits. Everything on it is reconstructed from public filings. This note explains what each source contributes, how the pieces were joined, what was assumed, and where the picture is known to be incomplete. It is written for researchers and practitioners who want to use or check the figures. This build covers the grant flows, the map, federal awards and USDA commodity food. Statutory goal tracking and community material follow in later builds.

What the map shows

Each line in the flow map is a grant that one organization reported giving to another: the giver's name, the recipient's name and usually its employer identification number, the cash amount, and the value of any noncash assistance such as food. Node size and ribbon width scale with dollars. Green is food (noncash), amber is cash. The map covers food and agriculture organizations across the State of Hawaii, the outside organizations that supply or fund them, and the local agencies that receive from them. It is a map of reported transfers between organizations, not a census of all food moving through the region.

How the organization set was defined

"Hawaii food and agriculture organizations" are tax-exempt organizations in the Business Master File with a Hawaii address that either carry an NTEE code beginning with K (Food, Agriculture and Nutrition) or have a food or agriculture word in their name: food, pantry, hunger, meals, kitchen, nutrition, feeding, harvest, glean, grocer, farm, farmers, agriculture, aquaculture, fishpond, loko ia, kalo, taro, mahi ai, garden, ranch, fishery, seafood, livestock, cattle, orchard, beekeeping, papaya, macadamia, coffee, breadfruit, compost, growers, produce. Name matches without a K code were then screened to remove unions, credit unions, employee trusts, congregations, botanical and ornamental gardens, animal sanctuaries and rescues, therapy and equestrian ranches, sports clubs, housing and community associations, and trade groups outside food. This yields organizations across every island. Foundations enter the map as givers when they report grants to a member of this set; organizations elsewhere enter only if they give to or receive from a member.

How flows are built

  • A flow is one row of a giver's Schedule I Part II or 990-PF Part XV. The giver decides the value. For food, that is almost always fair market value, and the two largest givers here state the method as a wholesale average per pound.
  • Recipients are matched by EIN when the giver reports one. Private foundations report no EIN, so their recipients are matched by normalized name and may occasionally be missed or misjoined.
  • When an organization filed more than one return for the same year, the later one (an amended return) is kept.
  • "Latest filing per organization" shows each giver's most recent tax year, so a giver's flows are never double counted across years. Selecting a single year shows only returns for that tax year.
  • A grant an organization reports to its own EIN is shown as "direct distribution": food the organization handed out through its own programs rather than through a partner.
  • Audited USDA food received by a food bank is drawn as a flow from a single node, "USDA TEFAP commodities (via Hawaii OCS)", using the most recent audit year.
  • In the Sankey layout, the few flows between two distributors are drawn to a recipient-side copy of the receiving distributor, labeled "as recipient", so the columns stay in order. Organizations beyond the "Named per column" setting are grouped, recipients by city.

Context (shown separately)10.555 National School Lunch, 10.553 School Breakfast, 10.557 WIC, 10.551 SNAP benefits. These dwarf the rest and reach households through schools, clinics and EBT cards rather than through the organizations on the map.

An award is attributed to the federal fiscal year in which it started, using its total obligated amount. Sub-awards are attributed to the year of the sub-award date. "Traceable" federal money for an organization is the sum of awards made directly to it plus sub-awards naming it; most federal food money reaches nonprofits through the state, so this is a lower bound. Audited totals from Single Audits are the more complete figure where they exist. In Hawaii the large prime recipients are the Department of Human Services (SNAP), the Department of Education (school meals), the Department of Health (WIC) and the Department of Labor and Industrial Relations, whose Office of Community Services administers TEFAP and the Community Services Block Grant.

The TEFAP layer

The Emergency Food Assistance Program is the largest federal food input to food banks and is absent from both of the other federal sources: the 990 folds USDA food into noncash contributions, and USAspending records almost no commodity awards. It is reconstructed from two ends.

  • USDA to Hawaii. Entitlement food is allocated by a formula weighting poverty at 60% and unemployment at 40%; Hawaii's weighted index is about 0.36%, so its entitlement is small (about $1.6 million of food in federal fiscal year 2024, $1.9 million with carryover, against $284,000 in administrative funds). Bonus and Commodity Credit Corporation purchases, roughly twice the entitlement nationally, are not allocated by state table, so Hawaii's share of those is shown as an estimate (national total times the index) and marked as such.
  • Hawaii to food banks. The state agency is the Office of Community Services in the Department of Labor and Industrial Relations, not the Department of Human Services. It contracts one eligible recipient agency per county: Hawaii Foodbank (Honolulu, with its Kauai branch), Maui Food Bank, and The Food Basket (Hawaii County). Where a food bank's Single Audit states the audited value of USDA food it received, that figure is used; the audited sum is a floor where a bank reports no food value or files no audit.
  • Reconciling the two. Audited sums can run well above USDA's entitlement figure. This is not an error: food banks value USDA food at the Feeding America national wholesale average per pound, while the entitlement is USDA's purchase cost and excludes bonus food. The two measure different things and are shown side by side, never added.
  • Separating food from cash in audits. The Clearinghouse records program names as auditors entered them. Rows flagged as direct awards from USDA are treated as food and rows flagged as pass-through from the state as cash; 10.569 is always food.

The map

The Map layout places organizations at their addresses over census tracts of the State of Hawaii, with an optional shading of each tract's food access or income indicators. It is the view most likely to be misread, so its conventions are strict.

  • A point is a mailing address, not a service area. A pantry's tract says where its door is, not where its clients live. Regional redistributors and headquarters are the sharpest cases: a food bank receives food at its warehouse and sends it to partners across its island and, by barge or air, to other islands; a statewide association receives at a Honolulu office for programs elsewhere. The "Hide distributors" control removes organizations that themselves give food out, so that the remaining points are closer to the last recorded stop.
  • How points were placed. Organizations with a street address were geocoded by the Census Bureau's geocoder to coordinates and a census tract. Organizations with only a P.O. Box, or whose address could not be matched, are placed at the average position of matched organizations sharing their ZIP code, or failing that their city, and drawn hollow. Organizations without any Hawaii address are not on the map.
  • What is not on the map, and why it matters. The largest single amounts have no destination point: food a distributor hands out through its own programs (reported as a grant to itself), the aggregate line for recipients under $5,000, and recipients named without an identification number. The note on the map states these for the current view. Because the missing recipients are disproportionately small pantries, an unshaded or empty tract can be a gap in reporting rather than a gap in service.
  • Shading and points measure different things and different years. The shading describes residents of a tract from the 2020 Census and surveys taken from 2020 to 2024; the points describe deliveries to organizations in the tax years covered. Placing one over the other invites a conclusion about mismatch between need and supply that the data cannot support. The map never computes food per resident, and readers should not either.
  • Dollars are the giver's valuation, not pounds or meals, and some large recipients are not pantries. A pet rescue that received food valued in the millions appears as a large circle. Hover or click to see what an organization is.
  • Religious congregations are a large share of recipients and serve members who may live elsewhere; 264 recipients have no organization type on record at all.
  • Restraint. Shading uses one sequential color, tracts are named by county and number, and the caveats stay on the canvas rather than in a footnote, so that a screenshot carries them.

Food security measures

  • Concentration: the share of all food given out by Hawaii food and agriculture organizations that passes through the single largest one, and the number of recipient agencies with only one recorded source.
  • Dependence: government grants as reported on an organization's own 990 (Part VIII line 1e, all levels of government) as a share of its total revenue, shown beside traceable federal awards and audited federal totals.
  • Where a cut lands: for each distributor with a funding base, exposure is that base divided by revenue (or, for the TEFAP base, audited USDA food divided by food given out), capped at one. A cut of c percent removes c × base from the distributor and is assumed to reduce each partner's food by c × exposure × that partner's current inflow. Results sum across distributors. This is arithmetic on reported figures, not a forecast.

Assumptions

  1. Reported grant values are taken at face value. Noncash food is valued by the giver, usually at a wholesale average per pound, and different givers use different rates.
  2. A giver's most recent return represents its current flows. Fiscal years differ between organizations, so "latest" mixes years ending between June 2023 and December 2025.
  3. Schedule I itemizes only recipients of $5,000 or more in a year. Smaller partners are absent, and an agency that appears to have one source may have several small ones.
  4. Organizations filing Form 990-EZ or 990-N report no grant detail, so they appear only as recipients even if they redistribute food.
  5. Recipient EINs are as reported by the giver. Name matching for foundation grants uses a normalized name and a prefix test.
  6. Federal awards are counted at obligation in their start year; spending may occur over several years.
  7. In the cut scenario, a distributor passes a funding loss to partners in proportion to current inflow and does not substitute other sources. Exposure is uniform across a distributor's partners.
  8. Hawaii's share of bonus and CCC food is assumed proportional to its entitlement index. This is an estimate and is labeled as one.
  9. Audit years are used as reported. A June year end and a December year end in the same "audit year" cover different months.
  10. An organization's mailing address stands for its location. Approximate placements (P.O. Box ZIP or city) are marked but still plotted.
  11. The map frame is the whole state; every organization with a Hawaii street address can be placed. Inter-island flows are drawn as straight arcs between addresses, not as shipping routes.
  12. County figures on the Islands and counties tab locate an organization by its address. Kauai's food bank is a branch of Hawaii Foodbank and files inside its Honolulu return, so Kauai shows no TEFAP food of its own and Honolulu's figures include it.

Labels and technical notes

  • Hawaii food or ag org (green): a member of the defined set. Outside supplier / funder (purple): any giver not in the set, including national food banks, foundations and donor-advised fund sponsors. Partner agency (grey): a recipient not in the set and not a giver.
  • Food (noncash) is the giver's reported noncash assistance, whatever its description; on this map it is food in nearly every case. Cash is cash grants.
  • FY on a flow is the giver's tax year as filed. FY on a federal award is the federal fiscal year (October to September). Audit year is the year of the organization's fiscal year end.
  • Other outside givers, Other Hawaii distributors and Other recipients in [city] are groups created by the "Named per column" setting. Hover for the count.
  • Federal: nodes in the Sankey aggregate traceable awards by program group; they are not organizations.
  • (direct distribution) marks food an organization reported granting to itself. (as recipient) marks a distributor shown on the recipient side of the Sankey.
  • In view figures respect the current filters; the header totals do too.
  • Dollar amounts are rounded for display (K thousands, M millions, B billions). Tables in the side panel show exact reported values on hover.
  • EINs are shown as reported. Organizations named only by a foundation, with no EIN, are marked "EIN not reported".
  • On the map, filled points are street-geocoded, hollow points are approximate. Point size is dollars in and out under the current filters. Low income and low access is USDA's 2025 designation by driving distance: a low-income tract where a significant share of residents live more than half a mile (urban) or ten miles (rural) from a SNAP-authorized retailer. Quantitative shadings use five quantile classes over metro tracts; for median household income the scale is inverted so that darker means lower.
  • The map's heat map of food received is a kernel density of noncash food received by organizations that do not pass food on, weighted by value and placed at organization addresses, with a smoothing radius of about three percent of the frame. Tracts by food received sums the same quantity by census tract in quintiles. Both exclude hubs, food banks (NTEE K31) and fund-raising or distribution cooperatives (K11, K12), even when those report no grants of their own, so their intake does not swamp their partners, and both show where recorded deliveries land, never where food is eaten. Flow arcs carry a moving dash from giver to recipient when motion is not reduced by the viewer's system setting.

Known gaps

  • Donors to an organization are not public. Schedule B is redacted in every public 990, so inflows are known only where the giver is itself a filer that itemizes grants.
  • Individual and direct corporate gifts never appear.
  • The Feeding America network's flows to other regions are outside the map; only the Hawaii-bound legs are included.
  • Sub-award reporting to USAspending is incomplete and capped per program; USDA commodity food appears in USAspending only as administrative funds.
  • Many farms, food hubs and cooperatives are for-profit or cooperative entities that file no Form 990 and appear here only when a nonprofit reports a grant to them.
